extracted.intended_audience: district court judges and patent litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for district courts on construing patent claim terms post-Phillips v. AWH, including the correct use and order of intrinsic and extrinsic evidence and common pitfalls that lead to reversal on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phillips methodology (order of consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look to the claims first, then to the specification (described as 'the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term'), and then to the prosecution history to determine the meaning of a disputed claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) controls claim meaning. Extrinsic evidence may be considered only after reviewing intrinsic evidence. The specification is the 'single best guide' to claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence controls
rubrics_metrics.description: The intrinsic record of the patent—the claims, written description and drawings (specification), and prosecution history—makes up the primary sources for claim construction and 'controls' over extrinsic sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should rely on intrinsic sources before using extrinsic evidence; extrinsic sources cannot be used to contradict an unambiguous claim meaning derived from the intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing limitations from the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts should be cautious not to import limitations into the claims from the specification, such as limiting a claim to a preferred embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read preferred embodiments into the plain language of the claims. Example: Howmedica Osteonics Corp. v. Wright Medical Technology, where the district court improperly limited a claim to preferred embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read claims in light of the specification to identify required limitations or specific definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the specification to determine if there is a specific definition or a required limitation that narrows the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification indicates a necessary limitation or 'fundamental object of the invention,' the court must incorporate that limitation into claim construction. Example: Praxair v. ATMI—specification required the flow restriction be sufficient to prevent a hazardous release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extrinsic evidence (dictionaries) is permissible but subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries and other extrinsic evidence are 'among the many tools' that can assist the court, particularly to 'better understand the underlying technology and the way in which one of skill in the art might use the claim terms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may rely on dictionary definitions when construing claim terms so long as the dictionary definition does not contradict any definition found in or ascertained from the patent documents. Consider extrinsic evidence only after intrinsic review and ensure consistency with intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rigid 'magic formula' or required sequence for sources
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no magic formula or catechism for conducting claim construction' and the court is not barred from considering sources in any particular order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexibility in sequence is permitted, but any extrinsic source used must not contradict intrinsic evidence. The recommended practice remains claims → specification → prosecution history → extrinsic evidence to minimize error.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claims are broad and specification discloses a narrow preferred embodiment, do not automatically narrow the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A common error is construing claim terms too narrowly by importing limitations from a narrow preferred embodiment disclosed in the specification even when the patent supports a broader interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify whether there is a basis in the intrinsic record for imposing a limitation; absence of such a basis means the plain language controls and broader reading may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer broader construction when genuinely in doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: When in doubt between two potential claim constructions, the district court should adopt the broader of the two potential constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has tended to alter claims to make them broader rather than narrower; adopting the broader construction when uncertain may reduce likelihood of reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is a question of law reviewed de novo
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit reviews a district court's claim construction decision with no deference (de novo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because there is no appellate deference, district courts should be careful and thorough in applying Phillips methodology and in documenting the intrinsic record analysis; this de novo standard contributes to possible reversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common appellate reasons for Federal Circuit review
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent reasons the Federal Circuit reviews district court claim constructions include: (1) patentees appealing a narrow construction for infringement reasons, (2) alleged infringers appealing a broad construction for infringement reasons, (3) patentees appealing a broad construction for validity reasons, and (4) alleged infringers appealing a narrow construction for validity reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of these typical appeal drivers when framing and explaining claim constructions, since different parties will appeal depending on the perceived effect on infringement or validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between failing to read claims in light of the specification and improperly reading in limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Two opposite errors exist: (a) improperly importing limitations from the specification into the claims (reading-in), and (b) failing to interpret the claims in light of the specification when a limitation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the specification supplies a specific definition or required limitation; avoid both extremes by grounding the construction in the intrinsic record and explaining the rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete district record can permit appellate resolution without remand
rubrics_metrics.description: If the district court's record is complete, the Federal Circuit in some cases may decide the dispositive issue (e.g., infringement) without remanding to the district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a complete factual and claim-construction record at the district court level to enable appellate courts to resolve issues where appropriate and possibly avoid remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries should be used to understand technology and POSITA usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries are useful 'to better understand the underlying technology and the way in which one of skill in the art might use the claim terms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dictionaries to illuminate technical meaning and POSITA usage, but corroborate dictionary meanings with intrinsic evidence and do not let dictionary definitions override the patent documents.
